title: Sub-gram insect robots—can they break free of power cords within two years?
dek: A National University of Defense Technology team built an insect robot that can fly untethered for four minutes, but it still can only control altitude and cannot turn. The field is stuck between ‘can fly’ and ‘can be useful’.
why: The first two-thirds covers insect-robot materials and mechanics—ideal for tech enthusiasts. The last third on human milk omics and biography discussion is skippable.
who: Engineers tracking micro-robotics and biomimetic engineering advances; researchers and healthcare professionals interested in maternal and infant health and milk science.
skip: The last ~10 minutes of chat about science biography books can be skipped—information density is low.

points.h: Even the CIA's Cold War insect robot was defeated by a stray breeze
points.body: During the Cold War, CIA engineers built a dragonfly-painted insect-sized robot equipped with a micro gas engine and eavesdropping equipment that could glide considerable distances. Yet even the slightest crosswind would completely blow it off course. The Insectothopter project ultimately failed. The field didn't seriously restart until the late 1980s.

points.h: Scale down to insects and physics becomes an entirely different game
points.body: At insect scale, gravity and inertia—crucial forces for large drones—become negligible, while static electricity and surface tension grow dominant. Air becomes so viscous that if you shrank to fly-size, walking would feel like wading through maple syrup. You cannot simply scale down large-drone components proportionally; the entire design logic must restart from scratch.

points.h: Direct wing drive cuts dead weight and friction for the Chinese team
points.body: Harvard's RoboBee and MIT's Softfly both use indirect drive—artificial muscles don't attach directly to wings, which amplifies motion range and reduces stress on fragile piezoelectric actuators. The National University of Defense Technology team does the opposite: direct attachment to test how far piezoelectric actuators can be pushed. This eliminates extra parts, reduces weight, cuts friction losses, and feeds all power directly into wing-flapping—the key to its cable-free flight.

points.h: Four minutes of untethered flight—but steering remains out of reach
points.body: The wireless insect robot's body is nearly weightless; almost all heft comes from battery and control systems. It achieves continuous flight for four minutes. But it can only control altitude; directional control is still lacking. The team's approach: achieve untethered flight first, solve controllability next. This exposes the gap between ‘can fly’ and ‘can be useful’ that currently defines the field.

points.h: MIT optimistically says two years, but batteries remain the deeper problem
points.body: Harvard postdoc Elio Chilita thinks wireless flight in two years is probably achievable, but flying longer than a few minutes will take far more time—because how batteries work at the fundamental level needs to change, something no robotics lab can solve alone. By contrast, MIT's Kevin Chen was the most optimistic interviewee, believing two years is feasible.

points.h: Supplementing during pregnancy isn't enough; lactation demands continued nutrition
points.body: Three intervention studies of undernourished pregnant women in low-income regions showed that locally-sourced balanced energy-protein supplements raised B vitamins and micronutrients in milk, but had little effect on total protein, fat, carbohydrates, or the milk microbiome and oligosaccharides. A critical policy implication: many programs supplement only during pregnancy, then stop after birth. This research shows continued supplementation during lactation matters equally, because it actually changes milk composition.

points.h: Breast health research was neglected so long it weakened cancer science
points.body: Milk and breast health were chronically underfunded research fields, and this neglect harmed breast cancer science itself—without understanding how healthy breast tissue works during normal lactation, understanding cancer remains limited. An intriguing correlation: each additional month a woman breastfeeds over her lifetime reduces breast cancer risk, but science is only beginning to understand why.

points.h: Eight biomarkers distilled from thousands predict the breast's overall health status
points.body: From thousands of milk compounds measured, researchers selected eight biomarkers that both respond to nutrition interventions and correlate with infant growth. The underlying proteins relate to female reproductive secretion, mammary tissue remodeling, milk synthesis, and inflammation signals. Collectively they signal not just what's in the milk, but how healthy the gland producing it truly is.
